coverage.note: Objectives, principles and requirement IDs are clear and traceable. Problems found: FR-8's tolerance has no unit, NFR-4's zero RPO conflicts with the stated architecture, payout changes break P9, and a confirmed decision depends on a pending backlog item.
Checked idempotency, the vault and PCI scope, the fraud hook, DR, latency, the HSM topology, reconciliation timing, the payout admin path, the state machine and the ledger against FR and NFR targets.

Several confirmed decisions in Section 24 (Redis key format, CVC handling, one HSM at launch, the batch-after-all-files rule, network tokens from launch) affect requirements. Each is framed as a refinement or as a question for a QSA or governance owner. Evidence for any formal challenge is attached later.

doc_anchors.quote: the final response is written to idem:resp:{idempotency_key} with a 24-hour TTL.

evidence.quote: the final response is written to idem:resp:{idempotency_key} with a 24-hour TTL.
on a hit, it returns the stored response immediately without touching DynamoDB or the Orchestrator.
merchants frequently use their own order or invoice identifiers, which is accepted.
A key that holds no merchant identity, combined with low-entropy merchant-chosen keys and no hash check on a hit, means responses can be served across merchants and the 422 rule is skipped.

recommendation.change_summary: In Section 9.2 and the Section 24 idempotency row, change the key to idem:resp:{merchant_id}:{idempotency_key}. Store request_hash in the cached value and compare it on every hit, falling through to the DynamoDB path when it differs. Extend the FR-5 test in Section 26 with a cross-merchant collision case and a concurrent-duplicate case.
recommendation.expected_benefit: Stops cross-merchant data leakage and enforces FR-5 on every path.
recommendation.issue: The fast-path cache key leaves out the merchant and the hit path skips the request-hash check.
recommendation.rationale: P3 and FR-5 require deduplication on (merchant, key) and a 422 when a key is reused with a different body.
recommendation.verification: Test: two merchants send the same Idempotency-Key and each gets its own payment; a modified body on a cached key returns 422.

findings.statement: Section 9.2 keys the fast-path response cache only on idem:resp:{idempotency_key} and returns a hit without any further check. This breaks principle P3, which scopes idempotency to the pair (merchant, key). Section 9.1 accepts order and invoice IDs as keys, so two merchants can easily use the same key, and one merchant can then be sent another merchant's stored payment object. Because a hit also skips the request-hash comparison, a reused key with a different body gets the cached response instead of HTTP 422, which breaks FR-5.
findings.title: Redis idempotency fast path ignores merchant scope and body hash

evidence.quote: Recovery point objective for authorized payments and ledger postings shall be zero, including on loss of an entire AWS region.
Replication is storagelevel and asynchronous, with typical lag under one second.
in-flight idempotency state is reconstructed from the payment table.
Asynchronous replication with non-zero lag gives a non-zero RPO when the region is lost, and the payment table has no idempotency key from which to rebuild state.

next_step.action: Decide between restating NFR-4 and a synchronous ledger design, and record the decision in Section 24.

recommendation.change_summary: Option A: restate NFR-4 as RPO of at most N seconds for regional loss (zero for AZ loss) and define reconciliation of the lost window against acquirer records. Option B: add a synchronous cross-region commit for ledger postings and accept the latency impact on NFR-2. In either case, add merchant_id and idempotency_key columns to the payment table (Section 19) so idempotency state can actually be rebuilt.
recommendation.expected_benefit: Gives NFR-4 an achievable, testable target and keeps FR-5 working after failover.
recommendation.issue: NFR-4's zero RPO conflicts with the confirmed asynchronous DR design.
recommendation.rationale: Either the requirement or the architecture has to change. Both cannot hold.
recommendation.verification: In the NFR-4 game day, inject a write load during failover, measure lost commits, and replay idempotent requests after failover.

findings.statement: NFR-4 requires zero RPO for authorised payments and ledger postings even if a whole region is lost. Section 20.2 relies on asynchronous storage-level replication with typical lag under one second, so committed postings inside that lag window are lost when the region fails. The section also plans to rebuild idempotency state from the payment table, but Section 19 has no idempotency_key column, so duplicate-charge protection (FR-5) is lost after failover as well.
findings.title: Zero cross-region RPO cannot be met by asynchronous Aurora Global replication

evidence.quote: Cascading does not move the p99 because fewer than 1% of card payments cascade
retryable outcomes - soft declines eligible for reattempt plus acquirer-side errors and timeouts - 3.8%.
acquirer HTTP 5xx; connection refused; no response within 2,500 ms
With 3.8% of payments cascading, more than 1% of payments carry at least two acquirer round trips, and any timeout cascade exceeds 2,500 ms, so the p99 sits above 1,500 ms.

next_step.action: Model the cascade latency distribution from the 2025 pilot data and set the deadline budget.

recommendation.change_summary: In Sections 11 and 21.1, add an overall deadline per payment (for example 1,400 ms) that stops any further cascade. Set the per-attempt timeout from that remaining budget rather than a fixed 2,500 ms. Re-derive the p99 budget with the cascade path included, or have the owner restate NFR-2 to exclude cascades.
recommendation.expected_benefit: Makes NFR-2 achievable and gives a correct latency budget.
recommendation.issue: The cascade latency and the 2,500 ms attempt timeout are incompatible with NFR-2.
recommendation.rationale: NFR-2 explicitly includes any cascade in the p99.
recommendation.verification: Run the NFR-2 benchmark with 3.8% retryable injection, including timeout outcomes.

findings.statement: Section 21.1 claims cascades do not affect p99 because fewer than 1% of card payments cascade. Section 10.5 reports 3.8% retryable outcomes, and the NFR-2 test injects 3.8%. With 3.8% of payments cascading, cascade latency falls inside the p99 tail. A timeout-triggered cascade alone takes 2,500 ms before the next attempt starts, which is above the 1,500 ms NFR-2 limit. As designed, NFR-2 is very likely to fail its own acceptance test.
findings.title: Latency budget assumes cascades fall outside p99, but 3.8% of attempts are retryable

evidence.quote: The Vault's KEKs are held in an AWS CloudHSM cluster with one HSM in ap-southeast-1a.
A second HSM will be added to the cluster when sustained card volume exceeds 1,500 TPS.
Card share of attempts (e-wallet ~30%, bank transfer ~15%) 54% 55%
55% of a 2,000 TPS peak is about 1,100 card TPS, below the 1,500 TPS trigger, so the single HSM stays in place for the whole design horizon.

next_step.action: Cost the two-HSM topology and propose an amendment to the confirmed Vault decision.

recommendation.change_summary: Change Section 12.3 and the Section 24 Vault decision to at least two HSMs in different AZs from launch, with the capacity trigger used only for adding further HSMs. Add an HSM-loss chaos test to Phase 9.
recommendation.expected_benefit: Removes a single point of failure for all card payments.
recommendation.issue: There is no HSM redundancy on the critical path for every card payment.
recommendation.rationale: NFR-3 availability and the three-AZ principle require redundancy, not a volume trigger.
recommendation.verification: Chaos test: terminate one HSM under load; card authorisations keep succeeding.

findings.statement: Every card authorisation needs a detokenise call that unwraps the DEK in the HSM, yet the cluster has one HSM in one AZ. If that HSM fails, every card payment fails, and cascading cannot help because every acquirer needs the Vault. The trigger for adding a second HSM is 1,500 card TPS, but at the 2027 design peak card traffic is about 1,100 TPS (55% of 2,000), so the trigger is never reached. This conflicts with NFR-3 (99.95%) and the three-AZ design in Section 20.1.
findings.title: Single-AZ single HSM is a single point of failure for every card payment

findings.statement: A single Finance user can both issue refunds and change the payout bank account, MFA is optional for that role, and the only notification goes to the user who made the change. findings.statement: Section 7.2 allows CAPTURED and SUCCEEDED to move to PARTIALLY_REFUNDED or REFUNDED, but it does not allow either of those states to move to SETTLED. A payment refunded before its settlement line arrives can therefore never reach SETTLED. Reconciliation (Section 16.2) cannot record the match, and FR-2 forbids an unlisted transition. Because refunded state replaces settlement state, CVC deletion and payout logic that key on SETTLED become unreliable.
findings.title: State machine strands payments refunded before settlement

evidence.quote: Journals are written in the same PostgreSQL transaction as the payment state transition that causes them, together with an outbox row.
No payment-path transaction updates a balance row, which avoids hot-row contention on high-volume accounts

findings.no_change_rationale: The design meets FR-10 and principles P1, P5 and P7 with an established pattern and checks the projection against the postings.
findings.statement: Journals, the state transition and the outbox row are committed in one PostgreSQL transaction. Balances are maintained as an asynchronous projection that is checked nightly against the postings, and UPDATE and DELETE are revoked on journal and posting. This directly meets P1, P5, P7 and FR-10, avoids dual-write inconsistency, and avoids hot-row contention at 2,000 TPS.
findings.title: Ledger is written in the same transaction as state changes, with an outbox and append-only enforcement
